chapter_title: Optimizing Imported Models: LODs, Occlusion Culling & Mesh Simplification
chapter_summary:
Creating visually rich 3D environments and detailed characters is a core skill for any Unity artist, but raw visual quality often comes at a performance cost. Unoptimized models can quickly bring even powerful hardware to its knees, leading to low frame rates and a poor player experience. Therefore, understanding and applying optimization techniques is just as crucial as the modeling itself. This chapter focuses on three key strategies: Level of Detail (LODs), Occlusion Culling, and Mesh Simplification.

**Level of Detail (LODs)** is a technique that swaps out high-polygon meshes for progressively simpler, lower-polygon versions of the same object as the camera moves further away. The idea is that distant objects don't need the same level of detail as objects up close, and rendering simpler meshes saves significant GPU processing power. To implement LODs in Unity, you add an **LOD Group** component to the root GameObject of your model. This component allows you to define multiple LOD levels, each associated with a different mesh variant. For example, you might have `LOD0` (high poly) for close-up, `LOD1` (mid poly) for medium distance, and `LOD2` (low poly) for far distance. You then drag your different mesh variants into these slots and adjust the "Screen Percentage" sliders, which define at what point (based on the object's size on screen) Unity switches between LODs. There's also a "Culled" state, where the object is no longer rendered at all. The key to effective LODs is creating distinct visual differences between levels that are only noticeable when the object is close, ensuring smooth transitions without "popping." Creating these different mesh resolutions is typically done in your DCC tool using decimation modifiers or manual retopology, though Unity's ProBuilder package or third-party assets can also help simplify meshes directly. A common mistake is having LODs that are too similar (no performance gain) or too different (obvious popping).

**Occlusion Culling** is another powerful optimization that works by preventing Unity from rendering objects that are completely hidden behind other objects (occluders). Imagine a player walking through a building: objects in rooms not visible from the player's current viewpoint shouldn't be rendered. This is distinct from frustum culling, which only culls objects outside the camera's view. Occlusion Culling requires a pre-computation step, known as "baking," because Unity needs to analyze the static geometry of your scene to determine visibility. To use it, you must first mark objects that will act as occluders (e.g., walls, large rocks) and objects that can be occluded (most static geometry) as **"Occluder Static"** or **"Occludee Static"** in their Inspector settings. Then, you open the Occlusion Culling window (Window > Rendering > Occlusion Culling), set your bake parameters (like "Smallest Occluder" and "Smallest Hole" which define the granularity of the culling), and click "Bake." After baking, you can visualize the culling in the Scene view. A critical safety note: Occlusion Culling only works for *static* objects. Dynamic objects (like characters or moving props) cannot be occluders or occludees. Incorrect bake settings can lead to objects disappearing too early or not culling effectively, so careful testing is required.

**Mesh Simplification** (also known as mesh decimation or polygon reduction) is the direct process of reducing the number of vertices and triangles in a 3D mesh. This is a fundamental technique for reducing the computational load on the GPU. It's often used to create the lower-detail meshes for LOD systems, or to optimize assets for performance-critical platforms like mobile, or for distant background elements. The goal is to reduce poly count while preserving the object's silhouette and important details as much as possible.
*   **DCC Tools:** Most DCC applications (Blender's Decimate Modifier, Maya's Reduce) offer robust mesh simplification tools, providing the most control over the reduction process. You can often specify a target polygon count or a percentage reduction.
*   **Unity's Built-in Tools:** Unity's ProBuilder package, while primarily a modeling tool, includes some mesh optimization capabilities. There are also various third-party assets on the Unity Asset Store specifically designed for automated mesh simplification.
The challenge with mesh simplification is finding the right balance: over-simplifying can lead to jagged edges, loss of sculpted detail, or a noticeable change in the object's silhouette, making it look blocky or low-resolution even up close. Always compare the simplified mesh against the original to ensure visual quality is maintained for its intended use.

By combining these techniques, you can build visually rich and complex scenes that still run smoothly. For example, a hero character might have high-poly LODs, but a distant tree might only have two LOD levels and be heavily simplified. Buildings in an indoor environment would be marked as static and contribute to occlusion culling, ensuring only visible rooms are rendered. These optimizations are not just for performance; they are an integral part of the artistic process in game development, ensuring your art is seen and experienced as intended, without compromise.

screens.title: Optimizing Imported Models
screens.subtitle: LODs, Occlusion Culling, and Mesh Simplification for real-time performance

narration.text: In this chapter we will learn three practical ways to keep your Unity scenes running smoothly without sacrificing visual storytelling. First, you'll learn the idea behind Level of Detail: replace expensive high-polygon meshes with simpler versions as objects move farther from the camera. Next, we’ll examine Occlusion Culling, which prevents Unity from rendering geometry that is completely hidden behind other geometry, saving G P U work in complex interiors. Finally, you'll learn mesh simplification techniques used to create those lower-detail meshes with minimal silhouette loss. Each technique answers a specific performance problem: distant detail, hidden geometry, and raw polygon count. I will also walk you through Unity-specific steps — adding an LOD Group, baking occlusion data, and choosing when to simplify a mesh in a DCC tool versus in-Editor. For example, a distant tree can be simplified aggressively and given just two LOD levels, while a hero statue needs careful retopology for close views. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like LODs that are too similar or occlusion baked with moving objects marked static. By the end you’ll know when and how to apply each method to improve frame rate while preserving the look you intend.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use LODs, Occlusion Culling, and Mesh Simplification together to reduce GPU workload while keeping visual fidelity where it matters.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement and tune LOD groups in Unity to reduce rendering cost for distant objects, understand and apply Occlusion Culling so that entirely hidden geometry no longer consumes G P U time, and identify when mesh simplification is appropriate and how to achieve it using DCC tools or Unity's ProBuilder. You'll also learn to balance art intent with performance, making conscious choices about silhouette and detail. You will also bake occlusion data for a static indoor scene and verify occluded objects disappear as expected. Finally, you'll practice comparing decimation results and deciding whether to retopologize a hero asset or use an automated reduction for background props. These skills matter because optimization is necessary for stable frame rates across platforms; without them, detailed scenes can cause poor player experience. Demonstrating these tasks will show you can both measure and reduce rendering workload while preserving the intended look.

screens.title: Level of Detail (LOD) — The idea
screens.subtitle: Why swapping mesh complexity by distance saves GPU time

narration.text: Level of Detail, or LOD, is the practice of providing multiple mesh resolutions for the same object and swapping them based on camera distance or screen size. The key claim is simple: distant objects do not need the same geometry detail as those close to the camera. By rendering simpler meshes for faraway objects you reduce vertex processing and fill-rate costs, which directly improves frame rate. A concrete example: a detailed statue may have a high-poly sculpt for up-close shots, a mid-poly mesh for medium range, and a low-poly silhouette for distant views. Implementing this in Unity uses the LOD Group component where you assign mesh variants to LOD0, LOD1, LOD2 and set the screen percentage thresholds that trigger swaps. A common misconception is that more LODs always equals better performance; not true. Too many levels or levels that are visually identical give no benefit and add authoring overhead. Another mistake is setting thresholds that cause popping — visually abrupt swaps. Use artist-driven mesh reductions that keep silhouette and key shapes, and tune screen percentages while testing with the camera. Takeaway: LODs give the largest wins where many copies of a model appear at varying distances, so apply them to foliage, props, and any repeated asset to multiply the performance benefit.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: LOD replaces high-detail meshes with simpler versions based on camera distance to reduce GPU work without losing perceived detail.

content.html:
Core Concept Level of Detail
What LOD is

Multiple mesh resolutions are authored and swapped by a runtime rule. The goal is to reduce triangles the GPU must process for distant, low-importance geometry.

Supporting points
  • LOD Group defines slots like LOD0, LOD1, LOD2 and a Culled state.
  • Screen Percentage controls when Unity swaps meshes based on on-screen size.
  • Create distinct visual differences between levels to avoid wasted effort.
Example
A park with hundreds of trees uses 3 LODs so distant trees render as low-poly billboards and close trees keep sculpted detail.
Key Takeaway

Apply LODs where a single asset appears many times at varied distances; tune thresholds to avoid popping and to maximize performance gain.

Visual: LOD Group Slots
LOD0
High-poly for close view
LOD1
Mid-poly for medium distance
LOD2
Low-poly for far distance
Common mistake
Creating LODs that are too similar defeats the optimization; create meaningful polygon reduction between levels.

screens.title: Creating an LOD Group in Unity
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step setup and tuning of LOD slots and thresholds

narration.text: Creating an LOD Group in Unity is a short, repeatable process. Begin by placing your high-resolution model in the Scene and selecting its root GameObject. Add the LOD Group component from the Inspector. The LOD Group exposes slots for each level and a Culled entry. Drag the specific mesh GameObjects or renderers for your high, mid, and low meshes into LOD0, LOD1, and LOD2 respectively. Next, adjust the screen percentage sliders that determine when Unity switches levels. A practical workflow is to set LOD0 to cover close ranges, LOD1 for mid distances, and LOD2 for far distances, leaving the Culled state for truly small-screen-size cases. After setting values, test by moving the Scene camera or entering Play Mode and observe transitions. A recommended practice is to use gradual thresholds and preview the transitions visually in the Scene view. If you notice popping, either tweak thresholds or improve the visual continuity between meshes. Example: if a lamp’s shade disappears abruptly at a certain distance, raise the threshold for the mid LOD or refine the low mesh shape. This process helps you validate the performance benefit while preserving the player’s perception of quality.

keyIdea.title: Implementation steps
keyIdea.text: Add an LOD Group, assign meshes to slots, set screen percentage thresholds, and validate via camera movement or Play Mode.

content.html:
Process Creating an LOD Group
Step-by-step
  1. Select the model root in the Scene and add the LOD Group component.
  2. Prepare or import high, mid, low mesh variants as child GameObjects.
  3. Drag each mesh's Renderer into the matching LOD slot.
  4. Adjust Screen Percentage sliders to set transition points.
  5. Test by moving the camera and fine-tune to avoid visible popping.
Example
A bench uses LOD0 from 100%–60%, LOD1 from 60%–20%, LOD2 below 20% and Culled under 2% screen size. Adjust until transitions are smooth.
Tuning tips
  • Make LOD changes where detail loss is least noticeable.
  • Avoid many tiny LOD thresholds; use 2–4 levels for most assets.
  • Test on the target platform; mobile devices may need earlier swaps.
Common mistake
Assigning renderers incorrectly or forgetting to include all visible submeshes can cause parts of a model to disappear at runtime.
Key Takeaway

Follow a repeatable series: add LOD Group, assign renderers, set thresholds, test movement, and iterate.

screens.title: Creating LOD Meshes — Tools and trade-offs
screens.subtitle: How to simplify meshes in DCCs and in-Editor tools

narration.text: Creating the actual lower-detail meshes is an artistic decision supported by several tools. In a DCC like Blender or Maya you have fine control via decimation modifiers or manual retopology. With decimation you often specify a percentage reduction or a target triangle count; this is appropriate for background props where exact edge flow is not critical. Manual retopology is slower but preserves sculpted detail and silhouette for hero assets. Unity offers some in-Editor options: ProBuilder provides optimization and limited simplification useful for quick iterations. Many teams also use third-party asset store tools that automate aggressive reductions. A concrete scenario: for a distant rock in a mountain range, an automated decimate to 20% of original triangles is acceptable because the rock's silhouette matters more than small surface detail. For a player-facing statue, do manual retopology to keep silhouette and UV layout intact. A common misconception is to rely solely on automated reduction without quality checks; always compare the simplified mesh against the original under expected lighting. Takeaway: choose a tool that matches the asset’s importance and budget time for checking silhouette and shading after simplification.

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Use DCC decimation for background assets, manual retopology for hero assets, and ProBuilder or third-party tools for quick in-Editor iterations.

content.html:
Definition Mesh Simplification
Where to simplify
  • Background props and distant foliage — aggressive reduction is fine.
  • Hero characters and focal props — prefer retopology to preserve form.
  • When creating LODs, use simplified meshes as LOD1/LOD2.
Tools
Blender Decimate Modifier — controlled percentage reduction.
ProBuilder — quick in-Editor optimization and fixes.
Third-party reducers — good for batch processing many assets.
Example and checks
After simplification, inspect silhouette and normals under scene lighting. Also check UVs if texture fidelity matters. If details collapse, back off the reduction or retopologize key regions.
Common mistake
Over-simplifying without reviewing silhouette causes assets to look blocky even at medium distances.
Key Takeaway

Match the simplification method to the asset’s importance: automated decimate for background, retopo for hero assets.

screens.title: Tuning LODs — Performance vs. Visual Fidelity
screens.subtitle: How to choose thresholds and levels without causing popping

narration.text: Tuning LOD thresholds is a balance between performance and perceived quality. The core decision is where to set the screen percentage breakpoints so the swap is imperceptible or at least acceptable. As an example, a low-frequency silhouette object like a lamppost can swap earlier because its silhouette is simple. A sculpted statue requires later swaps and smaller polygon reductions. A practical approach is to test on camera paths that represent gameplay: follow the player or run automated camera passes to see actual screen sizes. Contrast two mistakes: thresholds that are too conservative keep high-detail meshes longer and reduce gains; thresholds that are too aggressive create obvious popping and silhouette loss. Another useful tactic is to stagger transitions for complex objects — use a mid LOD that retains most silhouette features, then a far LOD for aggressive reduction. Use the Scene view to preview LOD transitions and tune until the visual change aligns with natural camera motion. Final check: measure draw calls and triangle counts before and after tuning to confirm the intended performance improvement. This comparison mindset helps you choose settings based on empirical results rather than guesswork.

keyIdea.title: Tuning
keyIdea.text: Set thresholds based on silhouette complexity and gameplay camera behavior; test with camera passes to avoid popping and measure performance change.

content.html:
Comparison Tuning LODs
Aggressive vs Conservative
Aggressive: Early swaps, large poly reductions, strong performance gains but risk of popping and silhouette loss.
Conservative: Late swaps, small reductions, less risk to visuals but smaller performance improvement.
Example
A distant rock can be aggressively reduced; a statue used in cutscenes should be conservative.
Practical test
  • Record camera paths and observe swap points.
  • Measure triangle counts and GPU frame time before and after.
  • Tune thresholds where swaps are hidden by camera motion or scene elements.
Misconception
Assuming automated tools set perfect thresholds. Human tuning is usually required for the best result.

screens.title: Occlusion Culling — Preventing invisible draw calls
screens.subtitle: How occlusion culling differs from frustum culling and why it matters

narration.text: Occlusion Culling stops the renderer from drawing objects that are completely hidden behind other geometry. Unlike frustum culling — which removes objects outside the camera’s viewing cone — occlusion culling analyzes the scene to find which objects are occluded from the current viewpoint and skips rendering them. This analysis requires baking because Unity needs to inspect static geometry relationships ahead of time. A concrete example: inside a complex building, rooms on the far side of walls should not be drawn when your player is in a separate room. To make this work in Unity, mark large static walls and obstacles as Occluder Static and mark objects that can be hidden as Occludee Static, then open the Occlusion Culling window and bake the data. A common mistake is attempting to bake dynamic objects or forgetting to mark occluders; occlusion culling only applies to static geometry. Also, overly aggressive bake settings can hide objects too early; set 'Smallest Occluder' and 'Smallest Hole' carefully and test. The main takeaway is occlusion culling is very effective in indoor or cluttered environments where many objects are simply not visible from typical viewpoints.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Occlusion Culling removes entirely hidden, static objects from rendering by precomputing visibility relationships during a bake.

content.html:
Core Concept Occlusion Culling
Why use Occlusion Culling

It saves GPU time by preventing draw calls for objects hidden behind occluders like walls or large geometry. Best used in interiors and dense scenes.

Key points
  • Requires a bake step so it only works for static geometry.
  • Frustum culling is complementary; occlusion culling covers hidden objects inside the frustum.
  • Careful bake settings avoid premature disappearance of objects.
Example
A player in room A cannot see furniture in room B; those items will not be rendered when properly baked and flagged static.
Setup reminders
  • Mark large geometry as Occluder Static.
  • Mark furniture and props as Occludee Static if they will not move.
  • Open Window → Rendering → Occlusion Culling and adjust smallest occluder and hole before Bake.
Common mistake
Marking dynamic objects as static to trick occlusion; moving objects will not be handled correctly and can disappear unexpectedly.

screens.title: Baking Occlusion Culling in Unity
screens.subtitle: Parameters, flags, and visualization steps for a reliable bake

narration.text: Baking occlusion data is an iterative process that requires attention to scene setup and parameters. Start by deciding which objects will be static: large walls, floors, ceilings, and any permanent architectural pieces should be marked Occluder Static. Then mark objects that can be hidden by those occluders as Occludee Static. Open Window → Rendering → Occlusion Culling and switch to the Object tab to verify flags. In the Bake tab, set 'Smallest Occluder' to the smallest object you want the system to consider as an occluder and 'Smallest Hole' to define the smallest pass-through the bake will consider. These values control granularity; smaller numbers yield more precise culling but increase bake time and data size. Click Bake and then enable the Scene view's Occlusion Culling visualization to inspect results. As an example, if you find objects disappearing too early, increase the smallest occluder value or adjust the occludee flags. Remember, occlusion culling is computed for static geometry only, so dynamic objects will require alternative strategies. The final step is to test in Play Mode along player paths to make sure visibility behaves as expected during real gameplay.

keyIdea.title: Bake process
keyIdea.text: Mark occluders and occludees static, set smallest occluder/hole values, bake, then visualize and test across player paths.

content.html:
Process Baking Occlusion
Bake steps
  1. Mark static occluders and occludees in each object's Inspector.
  2. Open Window → Rendering → Occlusion Culling and inspect Object flags.
  3. Adjust 'Smallest Occluder' and 'Smallest Hole' for desired granularity.
  4. Click Bake and wait for computation to finish.
  5. Enable Scene view Occlusion visualization and test camera movement.
Tuning tips
  • Start with medium granularity and reduce values if important occlusions are missed.
  • Increase 'Smallest Hole' if small openings cause too much culling complexity.
  • Re-bake after major scene edits.
Example
In a house scene, set walls as occluders and furniture as occludees. After baking, objects in other rooms should not render when walls block line of sight.

screens.title: Testing and Visualizing Occlusion Results
screens.subtitle: How to validate your bake and avoid disappearing objects

narration.text: After baking occlusion data, validating the results is essential to avoid gameplay problems. Use the Scene view’s Occlusion Culling visualization to see which objects are culled from specific viewpoints; culled objects appear differently so you can confirm correctness. Walk the player path in Play Mode and watch for unexpected disappearances. If an object disappears while visible, check whether it was mistakenly marked static or whether the bake settings were too aggressive. One common pitfall is marking interactive or animated props as static; they will not behave correctly with baked occlusion. A concrete test: position the Scene camera at expected player eye height and rotate slowly; if items that should be visible vanish, increment the Smallest Occluder or reduce the aggressiveness of the bake. Another practical check is to toggle static flags and re-bake to isolate which occluder caused the issue. Remember that occlusion culling reduces draw calls for static geometry only, so measure frame time and draw call difference before and after baking to confirm its effect. The final reflective question is: did the bake improve C P U/G P U workload without harming gameplay visibility?

keyIdea.title: Validation
keyIdea.text: Use Scene view visualization and Play Mode camera paths to detect and fix objects that disappear prematurely after baking.

content.html:
Verification Testing Occlusion
Validation checklist
  • Enable Occlusion visualization in Scene view and inspect culled geometry.
  • Walk or fly camera along player paths and watch for sudden disappearance.
  • Confirm dynamic objects are not marked static by mistake.
  • If needed, adjust bake parameters and re-bake.
Example fix
If an NPC disappears when visible, check its static flag. If flagged static, clear it and re-bake. If the issue persists, raise 'Smallest Occluder' so small gaps no longer create culling errors.
Measurement
Compare draw calls and frame time in the Profiler before and after baking to verify the optimization’s impact.

screens.title: Mesh Simplification — Reducing triangles without losing form
screens.subtitle: Principles and visual priorities when decimating geometry

narration.text: Mesh simplification reduces the number of vertices and triangles in a model while attempting to preserve silhouette and visual cues. The essential principle is to prioritize silhouette preservation and key surface features over micro detail. This means you often allow small surface details like fine creases or sculpted pores to be lost on distant assets, while preserving edges and outlines that define the shape. A practical example: a background building can afford collapsed ornamental detail, but its roofline and general proportions should remain intact. Tools like Blender's Decimate Modifier let you specify a percentage reduction or target triangle count, giving fine control over how much geometry to remove. If a simplified model looks wrong under lighting, consider preserving normal maps or baking detail into textures. A common mistake is applying a blanket percentage to every asset; instead, choose reduction targets per-asset based on screen importance. Takeaway: run visual comparisons under expected lighting and camera distances, and keep the simplified result only when the silhouette and perceived shape remain acceptable for the asset's role. Mesh Simplification — Reducing triangles without losing form means simplify meshes by preserving silhouette and major features while reducing surface detail that won’t be visible at target distances.. In practical terms, principles and visual priorities when decimating geometry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Principle
keyIdea.text: Simplify meshes by preserving silhouette and major features while reducing surface detail that won’t be visible at target distances.

content.html:
Definition Mesh Simplification
What to preserve
  • Silhouette and overall proportions.
  • Major edges and silhouette-defining features.
  • UV layout and shading cues where textures carry detail.
Example
A distant statue loses fine sculpted engraving, but keeps overall pose and outline so it still reads in the scene.
Workflow tips
  • Try automated decimation, then inspect and adjust.
  • Bake normal or detail textures if surface detail is lost.
  • Keep a version-controlled copy of the original high-poly mesh.
Common mistake
Assuming the same reduction percentage works for every asset. Each model needs evaluation against its viewing distance and role.

screens.title: DCC Tools vs Unity Tools for Simplification
screens.subtitle: When to simplify in Blender/Maya and when to use ProBuilder or asset store tools

narration.text: Choosing where to simplify meshes depends on your priorities. DCC tools like Blender and Maya give you pixel-level control, manual retopology, and predictable UV and normal outcomes. They are the right choice for hero assets where shading, UV islands, and silhouette matter. Unity’s ProBuilder and some asset-store reducers are convenient for quick iterations, batch processing, or when an artist needs to test simplifications directly in-Editor. A concrete example: if you need to reduce dozens of identical props for a level, a batch asset-store tool or an in-Editor reducer saves time. If you need to retopologize a character for deformation and texture baking, use a DCC application. A common misconception is that in-Editor tools are always sufficient — they are not for high-quality hero assets. The best practice is to simplify background and repeated geometry with automated tools and reserve DCC retopology for focal pieces. Always compare silhouettes, normals under scene lighting, and the performance impact to make an informed choice. DCC Tools vs Unity Tools for Simplification means use dccs for high-quality retopology and unity tools or third-party reducers for quick or batch simplification depending on asset importance.. In practical terms, when to simplify in blender/maya and when to use probuilder or asset store tools. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tool selection
keyIdea.text: Use DCCs for high-quality retopology and Unity tools or third-party reducers for quick or batch simplification depending on asset importance.

content.html:
Comparison DCC vs Unity
DCC Tools
  • Fine control over retopology and UVs.
  • Best for hero assets and characters.
  • Allows manual correction after decimation.
Unity & Asset Store
  • Fast in-Editor adjustments with ProBuilder.
  • Third-party tools can batch-process many assets quickly.
  • Good for level-building and tuning iteration speed.
Example guideline
Automate background prop simplification with fast tools. Reserve DCC retopology for characters and hero props where deformation, shading, and silhouette fidelity are critical.

screens.title: Lab: Create LODs and Bake Occlusion
screens.subtitle: Guided steps to apply LODs, mark static geometry, and run an occlusion bake

narration.text: This lab walks you through a practical unity exercise using a single imported model and a simple room to test occlusion. First, import a complex model such as a rock, tree, or small building into your Project. Duplicate it twice to create three variants for high, mid, and low detail. Simplify the duplicates in a DCC or use ProBuilder to create mid and low meshes. Drag the high-poly version into the Scene, add an LOD Group component, and assign the three variant renderers to LOD0, LOD1, and LOD2. Tune the Screen Percentage sliders and test by moving the Scene camera or entering Play Mode. Next, build a simple room with cubes for walls and floors, and mark them as Occluder Static in the Inspector. Mark props and the model as Occludee Static. Open Window → Rendering → Occlusion Culling, set smallest occluder and hole values appropriate to your room size, and click Bake. Finally, enable the Occlusion visualization in the Scene view and inspect whether objects in unseen rooms or behind walls are culled as expected. This step-by-step practice reinforces how LODs and occlusion work together to reduce rendering load in real scenes.

keyIdea.title: Lab focus
keyIdea.text: Create three mesh variants, set up an LOD Group, mark scene geometry static for occlusion, bake, and validate with Scene visualization.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity Create LODs & Bake Occlusion
Steps
  1. Import a complex model and duplicate it twice for high/mid/low versions.
  2. Simplify duplicates in your DCC or with ProBuilder for mid/low meshes.
  3. Place high-poly in Scene and Add Component → LOD Group.
  4. Assign renderers to LOD slots and tune Screen Percentage sliders.
  5. Build a simple room, mark walls Occluder Static, props Occludee Static.
  6. Open Occlusion Culling window, set parameters, and Bake. Visualize results.
Example checks
  • Move camera closer and farther to observe LOD swaps.
  • Enter Play Mode and verify occluded objects are not rendered.
  • Adjust thresholds and re-bake as necessary.
Key Takeaway

This lab puts LODs and occlusion together to produce measurable frame-time improvements in a small scene; iterate until visual issues are resolved.

screens.title: Combining Techniques & Performance Strategy
screens.subtitle: How to choose which assets get which optimization and why

narration.text: Effective performance optimization is strategic: not every asset receives the same treatment. Start by categorizing assets by importance: hero assets, interactive props, common repeated objects, and distant background elements. Apply retopology and careful LODs to hero assets. Use automated simplification and fewer LOD levels for repeated props and distant objects. Mark large, static architecture as occluders to protect interiors from unnecessary rendering; background scenery often benefits from both LOD and simplification. A concrete scene strategy: hero character uses 3–4 LODs with careful retopology and baked normal maps; environmental rocks use two LODs with a high reduction on the far LOD; indoor furniture participates in occlusion culling and can be aggressively simplified if not inspected up close. Misconception check: optimization is not purely technical; it's part of art direction. Always verify results under expected camera movement, lighting, and platform constraints. Finally, measure impact with Unity's Profiler: confirm reduced triangle counts, draw calls, and lower G P U frame time. The reflective question to end with is: which assets in your scene give the best performance return when optimized first? Combining Techniques & Performance Strategy means prioritize assets by role, apply appropriate lod and simplification levels, and use occlusion for static architecture; measure gains with the profiler.. In practical terms, how to choose which assets get which optimization and why. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Strategy
keyIdea.text: Prioritize assets by role, apply appropriate LOD and simplification levels, and use occlusion for static architecture; measure gains with the Profiler.

content.html:
Strategy Combining Techniques
Asset prioritization
  • Hero assets: manual retopo, multiple LODs, careful thresholds.
  • Repeated props: automated simplification and 2–3 LODs.
  • Background scenery: aggressive reduction and fewer LODs.
  • Large static architecture: mark as occluders for occlusion baking.
Example plan
Statue: 3 LODs with retopo. Trees: 2 LODs, billboards at far distances. Indoor furniture: static occludees and simplified models.
Measure and iterate
  • Use the Profiler to compare draw calls and frame time before and after changes.
  • Iterate thresholds and bake parameters until performance goals are met.
  • Document decisions so team members apply the same rules consistently.
Key Takeaway

Optimization is a targeted, measurable process. Prioritize assets, apply the right tools, and confirm gains with profiling data.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Quick references to the chapter’s essential ideas

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts you should carry forward. First, LOD is the practice of swapping mesh complexity based on camera distance to reduce G P U processing for distant objects. Second, the LOD Group component in Unity is the authoring tool you use to assign mesh renderers to LOD0, LOD1, LOD2 and set screen percentage thresholds to control swaps. Third, Occlusion Culling prevents rendering of static objects hidden by occluders and requires marking objects static and baking the visibility data. Fourth, Mesh Simplification reduces triangle counts using DCC decimation or in-Editor tools and must preserve silhouette for acceptable visual results. In practice, apply DCC tools for hero assets and automated reducers for background props. Remember to test changes with camera paths and measure results with the Profiler. These ideas work together: LODs reduce per-object complexity, occlusion culling removes unseen geometry, and simplification lowers the base cost of each mesh. As a final prompt, ask yourself which three assets in your current scene would give the largest return if optimized first.

keyIdea.title: Quick summary
keyIdea.text: LOD, LOD Group, Occlusion Culling, and Mesh Simplification together form a practical toolkit for runtime performance.

content.html:
Key Concepts What to Remember
LOD (Level of Detail)
Swap meshes by distance to cut GPU cost for distant objects.
LOD Group
Unity component for assigning LOD slots and screen percentage thresholds.
Occlusion Culling
Baked visibility system that prevents rendering of fully hidden static objects.
Summary
Combine LODs, occlusion, and simplification and measure gains. Prioritize assets by role and iterate on thresholds and bake settings for reliable results.

narration.text: Here are the short definitions to keep in your toolkit. LOD is swapping mesh versions by distance. LOD Group is the Unity component that orchestrates those swaps. Occlusion Culling prevents drawing static objects hidden by occluders and requires baking. Occluder Static and Occludee Static are the flags that include objects in the bake. Mesh Simplification, also called decimation, reduces triangles while trying to keep silhouettes. Frustum Culling is the camera-based culling that removes objects outside view and works alongside occlusion culling. Baked Lighting is separate but often paired with static flags to reduce runtime cost. Keep these terms clear so you can communicate optimization decisions with artists and engineers on your team. As a closing thought: clear naming and consistent static flag use will save you debugging time when visibility problems appear.

keyIdea.title: Glossary
keyIdea.text: Short, practical definitions of LOD, LOD Group, Occlusion Culling, occluder/occludee flags, and Mesh Simplification.

content.html:
Key Concepts Quick Glossary
Occluder / Occludee
Inspector flags that include objects in occlusion baking as occluders or occludees.
Mesh Simplification
Reducing vertices/triangles to lower rendering cost while protecting silhouette.
Frustum Culling
Automatic culling of objects outside the camera view; complements occlusion culling.
Closing takeaway
Use clear asset roles, apply the right tool for each asset, and measure changes with the Profiler to confirm real performance gains.
